title: The AI Recommendation Readiness Score
subtitle: This shows whether AI can only mention your brand or actually understand it well enough to recommend it over competitors.

questions.text: When someone asks an AI assistant to compare your brand against a competitor, what typically happens?

answers.label: It does not mention us at all
It mentions us, but the details are wrong or outdated
It mentions us correctly, but cannot explain why we might be the better fit
It gives one or two reasons we might be the better fit
It compares features, evidence and fit accurately enough to hold up in a sales call

questions.text: How connected are your brand facts, proof points and desired positioning across your published content?

answers.label: They live in separate documents that were never meant to connect
A few pages repeat the same claims, with nothing tying claim to evidence
Product pages cite proof points, but perception and support content sit apart from them
Facts, evidence and the perception we want are mapped for our top products
We maintain a structured map from facts to evidence to the perception we want AI to form, updated on a schedule

questions.text: If you deleted your top 20 pages of content tomorrow, would an AI system still know who you are?

answers.label: No, our entire brand story lives on those pages
It would remember our name and nothing specific
It would remember one or two facts, mostly outdated
It would recall our core positioning from mentions elsewhere
It would recall our positioning, our proof points and how we compare, from sources across the web

low.headline: Your brand is a pile of pages, not a knowledge map
low.text: Right now AI has facts about you scattered across pages that were never built to connect. My answer is always the same. Build a map from facts to evidence to the judgment you want AI to reach, starting with one product line.
steps: List every proof point you have for your top product or service
Connect each proof point to the specific claim it supports
Write, in one sentence, the judgment you want AI to reach after reading all of it

mid.headline: You have pieces of an ontology, not a full one
mid.text: Some of your facts and evidence already connect, though the map doesn't reach support content, reviews or comparison pages yet. Extend it past your own site.
steps: Audit which proof points already appear outside your own site
Close the biggest gap between a claim you make and evidence a stranger can find
Pick your next category and repeat the mapping exercise

high.headline: AI can already reason about you, keep the map current
high.text: You've moved past getting cited into something AI can evaluate and compare. The risk now is staleness, an outdated fact sitting inside a correct-looking answer. Put a review cycle on the map itself.
steps: Schedule a quarterly review of your facts-to-evidence map
Watch for outdated claims surfacing in AI answers about you
Extend the mapping method to your next two priority categories

questions.text: How does your team currently track AI search visibility?

answers.label: We don't track it at all
Someone checks a few prompts by hand when they remember to
We check weekly or monthly and record a snapshot
We check often enough to see the pattern change, not just one day's answer
We track visibility rate day by day, because we treat AI answers as a probability

questions.text: Which of these do you actually measure about what AI says about you: sentiment, reasoning, accuracy?

answers.label: None of the three
We glance at accuracy occasionally, nothing formal
We track accuracy and sentiment, but the reasoning behind the answer stays a blind spot
We track two of the three consistently
We track all three and use them to catch a wrong or outdated claim before a customer does

questions.text: In a normal week, how many hours does someone on your team spend manually checking how your brand shows up in ChatGPT, Perplexity, Gemini or similar tools?
questions.hint: Include screenshots, spreadsheets, or typing the same prompts by hand.

questions.text: What hourly rate should this time be valued at?
questions.hint: Use your own loaded rate or your team's. We'll multiply this by the hours above, then by 52 weeks, to show the yearly cost of doing this by hand.

low.headline: You're checking a rank that doesn't exist anymore
low.text: AI search runs on probability. It never held a fixed position to begin with. Checking once a month tells you almost nothing about the pattern. Start smaller and more often instead of bigger and more rare.
steps: Pick five prompts that matter most to your business
Check them at least weekly, ideally daily, and log what changes
Add sentiment and reasoning to what you track, alongside whether you appear at all

mid.headline: You have a snapshot, you need a pattern
mid.text: Weekly or monthly checks tell you where you stood on one day. The pattern, how often you show up and in what shape, is the number that predicts what happens next.
steps: Move your check-in cadence from monthly to weekly, then weekly to daily on your top prompts
Add sentiment and reasoning next to the accuracy number you already track
Use your hours and rate above to decide if a shorter check-in cycle is worth the added cost

high.headline: You're already tracking visibility rate, put that lead to use
high.text: Daily tracking across accuracy, sentiment and reasoning puts you ahead of most brands still staring at a rank that doesn't apply anymore. Use that lead to catch a wrong claim before a customer repeats it back to you.
steps: Set an alert for when an outdated or wrong claim about you appears
Share the pattern, not the snapshot, with whoever owns the affected product
Automate the repetitive part of this check to shrink the manual hours above

questions.text: Is your core brand story told the same way across YouTube, Reddit, LinkedIn, press and your own site?

answers.label: We only have our own site, nothing else carries the story
We're on a few other channels, but the story changes depending on who wrote it
The facts agree everywhere, but the framing shifts channel to channel
The story is consistent across most channels, with small gaps
The same core story repeats across our site, press, community and social in different formats, and we treat that repetition as the signal AI trusts

questions.text: For the topics you most want to win, do you run a repeatable cycle of making a claim, backing it with proof, and spreading it across channels?

answers.label: We don't have a defined list of topics we're trying to win
We have a list, but nothing systematic happens after we publish
We publish and back claims with proof, but distribution stays ad hoc
We run the claim, proof and spread cycle for a few priority topics
We run this cycle deliberately for the topics we picked to win, and can name the proof behind each claim

questions.text: Roughly how much of your team's time goes into the context layer, the reviews, forums, comparison sites and community answers around your own content?

answers.label: All our time goes into our own site, we don't touch anything outside it
We occasionally respond on review sites when something goes wrong
We spend some time here, under a quarter of our effort
We spend close to half our time here
We treat this as a major share of the work, because this is where AI decides what to trust

low.headline: One channel cannot carry your whole story
low.text: If your site is the only place your story lives, AI has one source to trust or distrust. Pick your strongest story and put a version of it in three more places before you build anything new.
steps: Choose the one story you most want AI to repeat about you
Publish a version of it on one channel outside your own site this month
Keep the facts identical across every version, even as the format changes

mid.headline: Same facts, different framing
mid.text: Your facts already agree across channels, though the framing shifts depending on who wrote it. Tighten the framing so every channel expresses the same message, just in a different format.
steps: Write one short version of your core story that every channel has to match
Review your last five pieces of content across channels against that version
Run one claim through the full cycle: state it, back it with proof, spread it

high.headline: You're repeating the story, keep picking your topics on purpose
high.text: You already treat repetition as a signal. Make sure it's aimed at the topics you actually want to win, not the topics that were easy to publish.
steps: Confirm your list of topics you're deliberately trying to win still matches your business priorities
Check that the claim-proof-spread cycle runs for each of them, not just your favorites
Retire a topic from the list once you can no longer back the claim with proof

questions.text: If an AI shopping agent tried to check your pricing or availability directly, instead of a person browsing your site, what would happen?

answers.label: Nothing but a person clicking through pages can get that information
The information exists, but only in a format built for human eyes (PDF, image, chat widget)
Some of it is available in a structured, machine-readable form
Most of our product and pricing data is available in a structured form an agent could read
An agent could read our data, complete a transaction safely and reconcile it with other systems, we've tested this

questions.text: Where does your current funnel put the moment a customer closely evaluates your options against alternatives?

answers.label: We assume a person does this step every time
We haven't thought about who or what does this step
We know some of this evaluation now happens inside an AI answer, but haven't changed anything
We've started shaping content specifically for that evaluation step
We design for a step where an AI evaluates and a person only confirms at the end, and we've adjusted our content for it

questions.text: How prepared is your site for a non-human visitor, something other than a search bot or a person?

answers.label: We've never considered this
We know it's coming but haven't audited anything
We've checked whether our site blocks or allows known AI crawlers
We've reviewed structured data, access and basic security for automated visitors
Our site is reachable, safe to transact with and compatible with outside systems for an automated visitor

low.headline: Your site was built for a person, not for what's coming next
low.text: An AI agent can't read a PDF catalog. Start where the cost of skipping this is highest, your pricing and availability, and make that machine-readable first.
steps: Pick your single most-requested piece of information (pricing, availability, specs)
Publish it in a structured, machine-readable format
Test whether a basic AI agent can retrieve it correctly

mid.headline: Some of your data is ready for an agent, most isn't
mid.text: Partial structured data is a start. An agent that hits a wall on your site will simply move to a competitor that built one that works.
steps: List which product or service data is still trapped in an image, PDF or chat-only format
Structure the highest-traffic pages first
Check basic transaction security for a non-human visitor, not only a human one

high.headline: You're built for agents, now prove it holds
high.text: Being reachable and structured for an agent puts you ahead of most of the market. Confirm it actually works end to end, not only in theory.
steps: Run an end-to-end test of an agent completing a real task on your site
Reconcile what the agent reports back against your own records
Repeat this test whenever pricing or catalog structure changes

questions.text: Where does your search and SEO team sit relative to PR, social and content teams?

answers.label: Completely separate, we rarely talk
We loop each other in occasionally, with no shared plan
We coordinate on big launches only
We share a plan for most major topics
Search, PR, social and content run from one shared plan

questions.text: When you publish data or a claim you want AI to cite, where does it originate?

answers.label: We mostly summarize what's already publicly known
A mix of original and secondhand material, with no clear rule
Original material for our biggest claims only
Most of what we publish is original, with sources named
We treat original data with a named source and a human point of view as what AI can actually trust and repeat

questions.text: Do you think of your search data (rankings, mentions, citations) as a report you send, or an asset you build?

answers.label: A report, we send it and move on
Mostly a report, though we keep the raw files
We keep and organize it, but nobody outside the team uses it
Other teams pull from it when they need to
We collect, clean and share it as an asset the whole company can use

low.headline: A split team already gives up half the game
low.text: When search, PR, social and content don't share a plan, AI sees a fragmented version of you, because that's what actually exists. Start with one shared meeting before you build one shared plan.
steps: Put search, PR, social and content in the same room for your next major topic
Agree on one story before any of them publish
Name original data you already own but haven't published anywhere

mid.headline: You coordinate sometimes, make it the default
mid.text: Occasional coordination on big launches leaves everything else disconnected. Widen what counts as worth coordinating on.
steps: Add a standing check-in between search and content before publishing
Turn your search data into something another team pulls from, beyond a report you send
Commit to one original data source you can publish on a regular schedule

high.headline: You treat search data as an asset, keep proving it
high.text: Shared planning and original data are what AI ends up trusting and repeating. It stopped being a one-time report a while ago, protect that by keeping the pipeline clean as you scale it.
steps: Confirm every team pulling from your search data understands what it means
Keep naming a human source behind your original data
Revisit team structure whenever headcount changes enough to re-create a silo

cta.headline: Want a partner who turns this score into an actual plan?
cta.description: Most people don't fail at the assessment. They fail at sequencing. In 30 minutes I'll show you which two things to fix first, based on your score and your stage. No pitch deck, just the sequencing call.

computed_outputs.label: Weekly cost of manual AI-visibility checks
Yearly cost if this stays manual

persona_selector.text: Which best describes your seat right now?

answers.label: I run SEO or GEO in-house for one brand
I run an agency or consult across multiple brands
I own the marketing or brand function, SEO is one part of my job
I am a founder and search is mostly something I read about, not run
